activities.caption: pin the start of the continuous record
activities.name: rsLandsatPlace

config.prompt: Landsat 1 opened its electronic eyes in which year?
config.why: July 1972 — since then, every piece of the planet's land surface re-measured every couple of weeks (every day for some sensors) for over fifty years without a break: deforestation, urbanisation, sea-level rise, groundwater loss and glacier melt became measurable, contestable, dated facts.

activities.anchor: Everything begins with the electromagnetic spectrum
activities.caption: file each behaviour: passive or active
activities.name: rsPassiveSort

config.prompt: Two ways to see from orbit — file each fact:

items.label: radar pulses, timed to the echo
laser flashes, timed to the echo
the reason it works at night and through cloud

config.why: The signal is digitised into a grid of pixels, each storing a number per spectral band — a slice of the spectrum the sensor is tuned to. Healthy vegetation looks dark in red bands and blazing in near-infrared, which is why it appears shocking red on classic infrared images.

activities.anchor: the familiar "photo" of a satellite image
activities.caption: drag the divider — snapshot vs data product
activities.name: rsPhotoCompare

before.label: The imagined instrument
before.text: A camera taking holiday snapshots from space — a picture you could look at directly.

after.label: The real instrument
after.text: Measured radiance, band by band, most of it invisible to the human eye — the pretty output is a reconstruction, and the reflectance numbers, ready for arithmetic, are the actual product.

config.why: One subtraction per pixel — the NDVI — already turns raw radiance into a drought-and-crop map for the whole planet: a satellite image is a spreadsheet wearing a picture.

activities.anchor: trade off against each other and against data
activities.caption: pair each programme with its corner of the balance
activities.name: rsTradeoffMatch

config.prompt: Four questions, four programmes — pair each with the corner it chose:

pairs.right: burns the planet daily at coarse detail to catch fires and ice motion the moment they start
sharpens where land management happens — 10 m pixels, about every 5 days
images essentially every land area daily
stare at one hemisphere continuously from 36,000 km

config.why: Spatial, temporal, spectral and radiometric resolution — finer and more frequent means more bytes, and the clever engineering lives in choosing the right corner of the four-way balance for the question.

activities.anchor: consequential open data decision in the field
activities.caption: call the usage explosion
activities.name: rsOpenEstimate

config.prompt: After the 2008 free-access moment, annual Landsat scene usage grew to roughly what?
config.why: Tens of millions of scenes annually, up from a few thousand — and a Kenyan analyst, a Brazilian enforcement officer and a Dutch PhD student now run on exactly the same archive, which is why the satellite record is global by construction.

activities.anchor: combining GRACE gravimetry and ICESat altimetry
activities.caption: pin the ice loss on the scale
activities.name: rsIcePlace

config.prompt: The northern hemisphere's great ice sheet sheds roughly how many gigatonnes of ice a year?
config.why: On the order of 270 gigatonnes a year from Greenland, around 150 from Antarctica — numbers with sea-level stakes attached, and unimaginable without satellites.

activities.anchor: The current decade added three things
activities.caption: line up the methane-hunting fleet
activities.name: rsMethaneOrder

config.prompt: From mapping to naming wellheads — sequence the methane era:
items: TROPOMI — continuous global methane mapping from 2017
GHGSat microsatellites pinpointing individual wellheads and landfill leaks
MethaneSAT launched by the Environmental Defense Fund in March 2024 to audit the oil and gas industry basin by basin
MethaneSAT lost contact in June 2025 after about fifteen months
config.why: Accountability with coordinates: a super-emitter is no longer an allegation but an address — and the fleet, not any single spacecraft, is the instrument.

activities.anchor: Persistent global imaging raises questions older than satellites
activities.caption: govern the audited forest
activities.name: rsPowerBranch

config.root: Your country's forests are audited from orbit each year, and the numbers are public.

start.text: How do you respond to the audit?

choices.label: Accept it — and contest the numbers with the same open archive
choices.feedback: Measurement creating accountability: anyone with a laptop can check a government's claims about its own territory. But a country audited from orbit has also lost the ability to simply deny the audit.

choices.label: Restrict overflights of your territory
choices.feedback: Dual-use tension never left: the same Landsat pixels that monitor crops monitor bases — and the first orbital imagery in history was military, Corona's film capsules of the 1960s.

end.text: The measurement is objective; what is measured, how it is processed into claims, and what happens to the people in those pixels are all human decisions.

config.why: Serious students should treat remote sensing as geography, ethics and geopolitics at once — and commercial constellations concentrate interpretive power in a handful of companies.
